analysis.one_liner: Curbs frivolous malpractice suits while forcing malpractice insurers to cut premiums and lose their antitrust exemption.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Rep. John Conyers with Rep. John Dingell and 4 Democratic cosponsors in March 2003, the bill was sent to a House Judiciary subcommittee on March 24, 2003, and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: Responding to sharp jumps in malpractice insurance premiums that were driving doctors out of some areas, this bill would have gone after the insurers themselves: it stripped malpractice insurers of their exemption from antitrust laws barring price fixing, required them to pass at least half of their savings from the bill on to doctors as lower premiums, and set up a federal price-comparison website. At the same time, it adopted some lawsuit-screening measures — a specialist's affidavit before filing, mandatory mediation, sanctions for frivolous suits, and a limit on punitive damages — but unlike the Republican bill moving in the House that year, it left patients' compensatory damages untouched. It also funded doctors in areas losing providers over insurance costs and created a commission to investigate why premiums had spiked. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients in areas where doctors were quitting practice over malpractice premiums would gain access to care, and anyone injured by medical negligence would keep the right to full compensatory damages while frivolous suits were screened out by affidavit and mediation requirements. Doctors would benefit from mandated premium reductions, antitrust enforcement against insurers, and federal grants toward their insurance costs in shortage areas.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and doctors facing premium-driven care shortages

how_it_helps.text: It required every malpractice insurer to dedicate at least 50 percent of the savings from the bill's lawsuit-limiting provisions to cutting physicians' premiums, with annual reports to the Secretary of Health and Human Services and civil penalties for noncompliance.
It stripped malpractice insurers of the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption, making price fixing, bid rigging, and market allocation illegal in the malpractice insurance business.

It preserved patients' right to full compensatory damages — the part of a verdict that pays for medical care, lost wages, and suffering — while limiting only punitive damages to cases involving gross negligence, reckless indifference to life, or intentional misconduct.

It authorized federal grants to help doctors cover malpractice insurance costs in areas losing providers over premium prices, and National Health Service Corps assignments to trauma centers at risk of losing their designation because surgeons and obstetricians had stopped practicing there.

It established a 15-member independent commission to investigate the causes of the recent dramatic premium increases and to study alternatives, including a federal malpractice insurance or reinsurance program and state rules letting doctors challenge rate increases.

For patients, it required an independent specialist's affidavit before a malpractice suit could be filed and mandated mediation, aiming to weed out non-meritorious cases without capping compensation for the ones that were real.

analysis.who_pays: Medical malpractice insurers would bear the direct costs: losing their antitrust exemption, dedicating at least half their savings to premium cuts, paying civil penalties up to $11,000 per violation, and providing quotes through a federal comparison site. Plaintiffs' attorneys would face new affidavit, certification, and sanction requirements. Taxpayers would fund the shortage-area grants and the independent commission.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposed new federal hurdles on malpractice plaintiffs in every state: a three-year statute of limitations, a required specialist affidavit filed with the complaint, mandatory mediation before trial, and mandatory contempt sanctions including fines and bar referrals for attorneys who violate the certificate-of-merit rules — all of which would have made it harder and more expensive for some legitimately injured patients to pursue claims.

The premium-reduction mandate relied on insurers estimating their own savings and self-certifying compliance, with a civil penalty capped at $11,000 per violation — a modest enforcement tool against companies deciding their own numbers.

Punitive damages would have been barred except in cases of gross negligence, reckless indifference to life, or specified intentional acts, and even then half of any award would have gone to a federal patient-safety trust fund rather than to the injured patient — a cap on recovery even in the worst cases.
The bill preempted state law on these procedural rules nationwide, overriding states that had chosen different approaches to malpractice litigation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's insurer-targeting side was strong and unusually concrete: repealing the antitrust exemption for malpractice insurers and requiring half of reform savings to go to premium cuts went after the pricing power that was driving doctors out of underserved areas. But its tort-limiting side had real costs an honest supporter had to acknowledge: a three-year federal filing deadline, a specialist affidavit required at the moment of filing, mandatory mediation, and contempt sanctions for attorneys would have made it measurably harder for legitimately injured patients — especially those who discover an injury late — to bring and sustain a claim, and the premium-reduction mandate leaned on self-certification with penalties capped at $11,000 per violation, which insurers could plausibly treat as a cost of doing business. On balance the bill traded some patient litigation access for a direct attack on insurer pricing, and it preserved the compensation rights that the rival industry-backed caps bill would have eliminated.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to two committees, then to a Judiciary subcommittee in late March 2003, and it sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers, joined by Rep. John Dingell, introduced the bill on March 12, 2003, as the Medical Malpractice and Insurance Reform Act of 2003.
The same day, the House referred it to the Judiciary Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee; no committee acted on it.
On March 24, 2003, it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was ever taken.
The bill died in subcommittee when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, without a hearing, a markup, or a vote in either chamber.

It attracted only 4 cosponsors, all Democrats, and the competing Republican malpractice bill, which capped damages rather than targeting insurer pricing, was the version that advanced in the House that year.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medical malpractice insurers, who kept their antitrust exemption and faced no requirement to pass savings along as premium cuts; the bill was never even voted on.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Malpractice insurers, untouched by new rules

for.name: Rep. John Conyers Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 12, 2003, pairing lawsuit-screening measures with antitrust and premium rules targeting malpractice insurers.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Health Subcommittee on March 24, 2003, and never scheduled it for a hearing or markup; it died there when the Congress ended.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Advanced its own malpractice bill capping damages awards (H.R. 5), which passed the House in March 2003, leaving no path for the rival Democratic approach.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat — Conyers, Dingell, and 4 Democratic cosponsors, with no Republican support — while the House's Republican majority advanced a competing malpractice bill focused on capping damages instead.

industries.note: The bill would have repealed their McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption for price fixing and market allocation, forced them to pass at least half of their savings to premium cuts, and exposed them to civil penalties — a direct hit to an industry whose rising premiums were pricing doctors out of practice. Its defeat left the industry's pricing power untouched.

New affidavit, certificate-of-merit, and contempt-sanctions requirements would have raised the cost and risk of filing malpractice suits, but the absence of caps on compensatory damages preserved the value of the legitimate cases that survived screening. Their interest in keeping damages uncapped runs alongside patients'.

Mandated premium reductions, antitrust enforcement against insurers, federal grants covering malpractice insurance costs in shortage areas, and Corps assignments to trauma centers all aimed at keeping doctors practicing where premium prices were driving them out. Patients in those areas shared the benefit.

The bill authorized National Health Service Corps assignments and shortage-area help for facilities losing their trauma designation because specialists had stopped practicing there — a lifeline for rural and underserved hospitals, funded by taxpayers.
